title: Life Originated Twice on Earth
gist: A Science Advances paper from a team led by Heinrich-Heine University argues life evolved twice on Earth, reached by tracing the evolution of the enzymes behind metabolism's 400-plus reactions back in time to origins near hydrothermal vents.

insights.claim: A Science Advances paper concludes life evolved twice on Earth rather than once, directly revising the working assumption that abiogenesis in our solar system was a single event.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: If a low-probability event repeated on one planet, the implied base rate for life arising elsewhere is higher than the single-origin prior allowed.
insights.quote: According to a new paper published in Science Advances life has actually evolved twice, right here on Earth.

insights.claim: The conclusion was reached by an international team led by scientists from Heinrich-Heine University in Germany, placing a European group at the center of a headline origin-of-life claim.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Notes where the methodological expertise for enzyme-phylogeny reconstruction currently sits.

insights.claim: The method treats metabolism as the one non-negotiable property of life — more than 400 complex chemical reactions organisms use to convert energy into usable form — and traces the enzymes responsible for those reactions backward in time.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A reusable method: pick the least-substitutable function of a system and date it, rather than dating the system's visible artifacts.
insights.quote: One “non-negotiable property of life,” the authors write, is our metabolism, the more than 400 complex chemical reactions organisms use to convert energy in a usable form.

insights.claim: The setting for pre-life chemistry is hydrothermal vents, whose surroundings created the primordial soup conditions the paper works backward toward.

insights.so_what: Reinforces vent chemistry over surface-pond scenarios as the default origin environment in current literature.
